blocks.x: Liverpool, NY barely takes up a square mile on the north shore of Onondaga Lake, but apparently that is plenty of room for an entire country’s worth of goodwill.

The tiny village just outside Syracuse has officially been named Reader’s Digest’s Nicest Place in America for 2026, beating out finalists across the country for a kind of community spirit that goes well beyond friendly hellos and borrowed cups of sugar.
We’re talking neighbors building wheelchair ramps, a cobbler repairing mountains of donated shoes, and a crawfish festival that sends every dollar back into local projects.
Liverpool is home to about 2,600 residents, yet more than 35,000 people pass through the village each day.

On one side, there are modest, tree-lined streets and independent storefronts with names like Knitty Gritty and Dead Ends. On the other, the lake opens up into miles of paths, picnic lawns, and the industrial salt history that helped put this corner of Central New York on the map.
The Village of Liverpool calls it a “delightful community.” Reader’s Digest just gave it a far bigger title.
Here’s why the little lakeside village is suddenly having a very big moment, and why it is worth putting on your next Upstate itinerary.

America’s nicest place is powered by people who actually show up

Reader’s Digest has run its Nicest Places in America program for a decade, asking readers to nominate communities where kindness is not just a slogan on a welcome sign. Its 2026 judges, including Al Roker, Craig Melvin, Mitch Albom, Mónica Guzmán, Sandra Clark, and restaurateur Molly Irani, selected Liverpool because support there seems to happen everywhere at once.
At the heart of the story is Operation Northern Comfort, a Liverpool-born nonprofit with a distinctly unlikely origin story.

It began in 2005 as Operation Southern Comfort, when the late local volunteer Norm “Mr. Liverpool” Andrzejewski started sending Central New Yorkers to Louisiana after Hurricane Katrina. Over six years, the group made repeated trips south, helping rebuild homes, deliver supplies, plant trees, and give local school bands donated instruments.
Then, in 2012, the organization shifted its attention north.

Today, Operation Northern Comfort uses that same volunteer muscle to build wheelchair ramps and lifts, widen doorways, repair bathrooms, and take on custom projects for local residents who need help navigating their homes. In 2025 alone, the group completed 57 projects, funded largely by its annual Crawfish Festival, a Central New York party that draws more than 6,000 people to Syracuse’s Clinton Square each May.
The cobbler whose shoe drive hit 300,000 pairs
Then there is Ralph Rotella, a Liverpool resident and old-school cobbler whose story is the sort of thing that makes the designation make immediate sense.

Rotella runs Discount Shoe Repair in downtown Syracuse, and for years he has collected donated shoes, restored what he can, and given them to the Syracuse Rescue Mission for people who need them. Boots, sneakers, loafers, dress shoes, mismatched bags dropped at the shop, even bags left at his front door in Liverpool, all of it adds up.

Last December, his annual collection passed 300,000 pairs of shoes since 2011, including a single-year record of more than 45,000 pairs in 2025. The work is supported by a rotating cast of people who donate footwear, buy a new pair for the drive, or show up simply because they know the cobbler who keeps the effort moving.

Getty Images / M. Suhail
It also sits beside one of Central New York’s best lakefront parks
The community story is the reason for the national title, but Liverpool does not exactly make it hard to understand why people stick around.

The village sits on the north shore of Onondaga Lake, with Onondaga Lake Park acting as its backyard. The waterfront greenway is sometimes called the “Central Park of Central New York,” with more than eight miles of paved trails running beside the lake for walking, biking, jogging, skating, and general staring-at-the-water purposes.

Picture a flat lakeside path, runners and cyclists rolling by, picnic tables facing the water, and the Syracuse skyline sitting quietly in the distance to the south. There is a marina, playgrounds, a skate park, dog park, and enough open lawn to make a sunny Central New York afternoon feel unexpectedly spacious.

The lake also carries serious cultural and environmental weight. Reader’s Digest notes that its shores were once a place where the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca peoples brokered peace. After decades of industrial pollution, extensive restoration efforts have made the lake fishable again, and birders now come to spot the eagle’s nest near the Skä- noñh Great Law of Peace Center.
Salt, hot dogs, and a Hollywood-ready high school
Despite its small radius relatively, there’s plenty happening here that catches at the eye, especially if passing through on your next trip to the 315.

Starting with the Salt Museum, a small, seasonal museum inside Onondaga Lake Park that sits on the site of an original salt-boiling block. This stretch of shoreline was once part of the massive salt industry that gave nearby Syracuse its enduring “Salt City” nickname, producing the white crystals that helped fuel the region’s 19th-century economy. Today, admission is free, and the museum makes for an easy detour between a walk along the lake and lunch.

Then there’s lunch at Heid’s of Liverpool, the neon-lit roadside hot dog institution that has been feeding Central New Yorkers since 1917. Just minutes from the lake, the counter-service stand is famous for grilled dogs, including regional white hots, piled with chili, sauerkraut, and whatever else feels right after an afternoon outdoors. Root beer floats are also very much part of the equation.

And finally Liverpool’s wildest little plot twist: American High, the production company that transformed the former A.V. Zogg Middle School into Syracuse Studios. The old school now holds 100,000 square feet of camera-ready classrooms, lockers, offices, and soundstage space, giving teen movies the slightly surreal advantage of being filmed in an actual former school building.
Planning a visit from NYC

Liverpool is roughly a four-and-a-half to five hour to drive from NYC, depending on traffic and your starting point, making it better suited to a long weekend or a stop within a broader Syracuse and Finger Lakes getaway than a quick same-day escape.
The destination is not selling one flashy must-see attraction, and that is kind of the point.
Go for the lake loop. Walk through the free Salt Museum. Eat a hot dog under Heid’s neon. But also talk to the people around, because that’s what’s ultimately earned them the title.
